Nineteen first-year students participated. Resource persons Galety Mohammad Gouse, Zabdiel Tan, and Seth Vidreo explained how an IT company operates and how interns would benefit from the Center. meta.commentText: In this collaborative exercise, intern teams will develop, deliver, and critically assess project-based PowerPoint presentations. The process is divided into three key phases: preparation, presentation, and peer evaluation.   1. Team Preparation of PowerPoint Presentations Each team will create a clear, concise, and visually supportive PowerPoint presentation that effectively communicates the objectives, methodology, findings, and conclusions of their project. Teams are expected to: Structure content logically: Include a title slide, agenda, problem statement, methods, key results/discussion, conclusions, and next steps or recommendations. Design for clarity: Use bullet points, visuals (charts, diagrams, images), and minimal text per slide to reinforce spoken explanations—not replace them. Coordinate roles: Assign team members to present specific sections, ensuring smooth transitions and cohesive delivery. Time management: Adhere to the designated time limit (e.g., 10–15 minutes) to allow for Q&A and feedback.   2. Team Presentation Delivery Each team will present their slides to the class or evaluation panel. During the presentation, the presenting team should: - Speak clearly and engage the audience. - Avoid simply reading slides; instead, elaborate on key points. - Manage timing and transitions professionally. - Respond to questions thoughtfully during a brief Q&A session following the presentation.   3. Peer Evaluation & Feedback While teams present, all other teams act as active evaluators. Their role is to observe critically and provide constructive feedback. Each evaluating team will complete a structured evaluation form (digital or paper) addressing criteria such as: Content quality: Depth, accuracy, relevance, and logical flow. Slide design: Readability, visual appeal, effective use of graphics, and minimal text overload. Delivery: Clarity, pace, eye contact, teamwork, and time management. Q&A performance: Ability to answer questions clearly and confidently.  After all presentations, or immediately following each one (as directed), evaluating teams will share written or verbal feedback. Feedback must be: Specific (e.g., “The diagram on slide 5 clarified the process well” rather than “Good job”). Constructive (e.g., “Consider reducing text on slide 3 and using a graph instead”). Respectful and professional, focusing on the work, not the individuals.   Goals of the Process For presenting teams: Gain experience in public speaking, visual communication, and handling questions under real-time observation. For evaluating teams: Develop critical thinking, active listening, and the ability to articulate constructive feedback—key skills in collaborative work environments.   Outcome All teams will receive a compilation of peer feedback along with the instructor's evaluation. This multi-source input helps identify strengths and areas for improvement, fostering a learning environment grounded in mutual respect and continuous growth.

meta.commentText: Day 6 is focused on bridging user-facing design with disciplined backend coding practices. Interns will begin by translating their project requirements into tangible front-end layouts, then shift focus to mastering Test-Driven Development (TDD) – a professional methodology that prioritizes writing tests before implementation code.   Morning Session (9:00 AM – 10:45 AM): Front-End Design Development  Interns will work on developing the front-end design of their assigned projects. This session emphasizes creating intuitive, responsive, and visually coherent user interfaces based on previously defined project specifications.  Key activities include:  - Translating wireframes or mockups into functional front-end code (HTML/CSS/JavaScript, or the framework specified for the project) - Ensuring layout consistency, navigation clarity, and basic interactivity - Applying principles of user experience (UX) such as logical information hierarchy and visual feedback - Preparing to integrate the front end with backend logic in subsequent days  Deliverable by end of this session: A working draft of the core front-end interface for each project.     Tea Break (10:45 AM – 11:00 AM)  A 15-minute break for interns to refresh before transitioning into the backend-focused TDD module.     Late Morning Session (11:00 AM – 12:30 PM): Introduction to Test-Driven Development (TDD)  This hands-on session introduces the Test-Driven Development (TDD) philosophy – a professional software development practice where tests are written before the actual code. Interns will learn by doing, starting with a simple product function before applying TDD to a Depth-First Search (DFS) algorithm.  Part 1: TDD Philosophy & Practice (11:00 AM – 11:45 AM)  - Concept introduction: Explain the Red-Green-Refactor cycle:   - Red – Write a failing test for a desired feature   - Green – Write the minimal code to pass the test   - Refactor – Improve the code while keeping tests green - Guided practice: Interns implement a simple product function (e.g., `multiply(a, b)`) using TDD, writing tests first, then the function, then refactoring.  Part 2: Applying TDD to Depth-First Search (DFS) (11:45 AM – 12:30 PM)  Building on the TDD rhythm, interns will apply TDD principles to implement a Depth-First Search algorithm on a graph or tree structure.  Steps:  1. Write a failing test for a specific DFS behavior (e.g., visiting nodes in correct order, finding a target value) 2. Implement just enough DFS code to pass the test 3. Refactor for clarity and efficiency 4. Repeat for edge cases (empty graph, missing node, cyclic graphs)  Learning outcomes:  - Understand how TDD leads to cleaner, more testable, and more reliable code - Gain confidence in writing tests before implementation - Apply systematic testing to recursive algorithms like DFS     Wrap-Up (12:30 PM)  Brief recap of the day's accomplishments: completed front-end drafts, hands-on TDD practice, and a tested DFS implementation. Instructors will provide pointers for further practice before the next session.    Overall Goal for Day 6:   By the end of the day, interns will have made tangible progress on their project's user interface and adopted a professional testing discipline (TDD) that they can apply to all future coding tasks, starting with graph algorithms like DFS.

meta.commentText: Session Overview  This session deepens interns' mastery of Test-Driven Development (TDD) by continuing hands-on work with the Depth-First Search (DFS) algorithm. Following individual practice, interns will transition into group collaboration to systematically identify, write, and test edge cases – a critical skill for building robust, production-ready software.   Part 1: Continued TDD Practice with DFS (09:00 – 09:45)  Building on prior introductory work, interns will further develop their DFS implementation using the Red-Green-Refactor cycle.  Activities:  - Expand the DFS algorithm to handle additional requirements, such as:   - Returning the order of visited nodes   - Searching for a specific target value   - Handling different graph representations (adjacency list vs. matrix) - Write new tests first for each desired behavior, then implement just enough code to pass - Refactor existing DFS code for improved efficiency, readability, and recursion safety (e.g., avoiding stack overflow on deep graphs)  Key TDD principles reinforced:  - Never write new functionality without a failing test first - Keep the cycle short (seconds to a few minutes per iteration) - Trust the tests – refactor fearlessly when tests are green   Part 2: Group Collaboration on Edge Cases for Unit Tests (09:45 – 10:30)  Interns will form small teams (3–4 members) to systematically explore and test edge cases for DFS. This collaborative approach surfaces scenarios that individuals might overlook and mirrors real-world code review practices.  Collaboration process:  1. Brainstorm edge cases for DFS on graphs/trees, such as:    - Empty graph (no nodes)    - Single node graph    - Disconnected graphs (components with no paths between them)    - Cyclic graphs (preventing infinite loops)    - Very deep graphs (testing recursion limits)    - Graphs with duplicate values or self-loops    - Null or invalid inputs  2. Write unit tests collaboratively for each edge case (still following TDD principles).    - One intern writes a failing test, teammates review it for correctness and clarity    - Another intern implements the minimal code to pass the test    - The group refactors together, discussing trade-offs  3. Run the full test suite and analyze results.    - Identify gaps in test coverage    - Discuss why certain edge cases break naive DFS implementations    - Document lessons learned about defensive programming   Learning Outcomes  By the end of this session, interns will be able to:  - Confidently apply TDD to recursive algorithms like DFS - Identify, prioritize, and test edge cases that typical implementations miss - Collaborate effectively on unit test design and code implementation - Appreciate how group testing improves code reliability and catches bugs early   Deliverable  Each group will produce: - A completed DFS implementation with a comprehensive suite of unit tests covering standard cases and edge cases - A brief written summary (2–3 bullet points) of the most surprising or instructive edge case encountered
